faq.a: No; early Graves’ or T3‑toxicosis may have normal TSH. Check free T3/T4 if suspicion remains.
faq.q: Can a normal TSH rule out hyperthyroidism?

faq.a: It carries a higher risk of severe liver injury and agranulocytosis compared with methimazole.
faq.q: Why avoid propylthiouracil in most patients?

faq.a: Excess iodine can precipitate hyperthyroidism in autonomous nodules; give only when deficiency is proven.

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman presents with weight loss, tremor, and a diffuse goitre. TSH is 0.03 mIU/L, free T4 is 2.5 × ULN. What is the next best step? — Start a thionamide (methimazole) and a beta‑blocker while arranging definitive therapy.

A patient on amiodarone develops fatigue and cold intolerance; TSH is 12 mIU/L, free T4 is low. How does amiodarone cause hypothyroidism? — Excess iodine from amiodarone induces the Wolff‑Chaikoff effect, suppressing hormone synthesis.

In a region with endemic iodine deficiency, a child has a goitre but normal TSH and free T4. What does this indicate? — Subclinical iodine deficiency; advise iodised salt and monitor thyroid function.

A 60‑year‑old man with known Graves’ disease presents with fever, tachycardia, and altered consciousness. Which lab pattern confirms thyroid storm? — Suppressed TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) with markedly elevated free T4/T3; treat as emergency.
Why is measuring free T4 preferred over total T4 in patients with low albumin? — Free T4 reflects the biologically active hormone independent of binding protein variations.

A patient with painless thyroiditis shows low TSH and low free T4. How do you differentiate this from Graves’ disease? — Absence of TSH‑receptor antibodies and low radioactive iodine uptake (if available) point to thyroiditis.
What are the contraindications for beta‑blocker use in hyperthyroid patients? — Severe asthma, bradycardia, or heart block; choose alternative symptom control.

How would you monitor a patient on levothyroxine after thyroidectomy in a low‑resource setting? — Check TSH and free T4 at 6‑8 weeks, then every 6–12 months; adjust dose clinically if labs unavailable.
ai.title: Thyroid Hormone Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Thyroid chemical pathology examines how altered synthesis, metabolism, or transport of thyroid hormones produces clinical disease. Understanding patterns of hormone levels guides diagnosis and treatment, especially where tests are limited.

b: Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH, low free T4
Primary hyperthyroidism: low TSH, high free T4/T3
Central (secondary) disorders: abnormal TSH with inappropriately low or high thyroid hormones
sections.p: Thyroid chemical pathology refers to the quantitative and qualitative assessment of thyroid hormones (T4, T3) and regulatory proteins (TSH, thyroglobulin, thyroid antibodies). Diagnosis rests on interpreting these results in context.

t.b: Is the pituitary response appropriate? Low suggests hyperthyroidism or pituitary suppression; high suggests hypothyroidism or pituitary over‑activity

t.a: Free T4 (or total T4 if free not available)
t.b: What is the circulating hormone level? Low confirms hypothyroidism; high confirms hyperthyroidism
Helps identify T3‑toxicosis or assess severity of hyperthyroidism
Is the disease autoimmune? Positive antibodies support Hashimoto’s or Graves’ disease
Is there residual or recurrent thyroid tissue? Rising levels suggest recurrence

b: Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH 4.5–10 mIU/L, normal free T4
Overt hypothyroidism: TSH >10 mIU/L, free T4 below reference
Mild hyperthyroidism: TSH <0.1 mIU/L, free T4 1–2 × upper limit
Thyroid storm: severe tachycardia, fever, altered mental status, TSH suppressed, free T4 markedly elevated
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and hormone derangement; for hypothyroidism, the WHO classification (subclinical vs overt) is used. For hyperthyroidism, the Graves’ Ophthalmopathy score and presence of thyroid storm are key.

b: Iodine deficiency (goitre, hypothyroidism)
Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s) – common in women
Graves’ disease (autoimmune hyperthyroidism)
Post‑iodine supplementation excess
Thyroiditis after viral infection (subacute, painless)
Medication‑induced (e.g., amiodarone, lithium)
Tuberculosis of the thyroid (rare but reported)
Herbal remedies containing goitrogens
sections.p: Identify the most common aetiologies in low‑resource East African settings before rarer causes.

b: Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, delayed reflexes, goitre may be present
Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, anxiety, goitre, ophthalmopathy in Graves’
sections.p: Clinical clues often precede lab confirmation; pattern differs between hypo‑ and hyper‑thyroidism.
Prioritise tests that answer the clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is the axis suppressed or over‑active? If unavailable, use clinical scoring and total T4
Quantifies hormone excess or deficiency; if not available, total T4 with albumin correction can be used
Detects T3‑toxicosis; if unavailable, rely on clinical severity and TSH
Distinguish autoimmune from other causes; if unavailable, use clinical features (e.g., ophthalmopathy for Graves’)
Differentiates Graves’ (high uptake) from thyroiditis (low uptake); if unavailable, use ESR and pain to suggest thyroiditis

b: Thyroid storm: fever, delirium, heart failure – treat immediately
Myxedema coma: hypothermia, altered consciousness, respiratory depression – emergency care
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response in hyperthyroidism
Severe hypercalcemia from hyperthyroidism
sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening derangements that need urgent action.

b: Hypothyroidism: start levothyroxine (synthetic T4) – replaces missing hormone; avoid liothyronine alone due to rapid fluctuations
Hyperthyroidism (Graves’): thionamides (methimazole preferred) inhibit hormone synthesis; avoid propylthiouracil where liver toxicity risk is high
Beta‑blockers (e.g., propranolol) for symptom control – also reduce peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
Iodine deficiency: give iodised salt or oral potassium iodide in acute deficiency
Post‑radioiodine or surgery: lifelong levothyroxine replacement
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then correct hormone levels while monitoring for adverse effects.

b: Check TSH and free T4 6–8 weeks after initiating or changing therapy, then every 6–12 months
Educate patients on iodised salt use and avoidance of goitrogenic herbs
Screen pregnant women early for thyroid dysfunction
Monitor for atrial fibrillation in hyperthyroid patients
sections.p: Regular monitoring ensures stable hormone levels and detects complications early.

b: Anxiety disorder vs hyperthyroidism – both cause tremor and palpitations; thyroid labs differentiate
Depression vs hypothyroidism – overlapping fatigue and weight change; check TSH
Pituitary adenoma vs secondary hypothyroidism – low TSH with low T4; MRI needed if pituitary disease suspected

b: Non‑thyroidal illness syndrome: low T3, normal TSH – does not indicate true hypothyroidism
Biotin supplementation can falsely lower TSH and raise free T4 on immunoassays
Pregnancy increases thyroid‑binding globulin, raising total T4 while free T4 remains normal

whenToSeekHelp: Altered mental status with fever (possible thyroid storm)
Severe hypothermia, bradycardia, or respiratory failure (myxedema coma)
New onset atrial fibrillation with rapid rate
